claims.text: The initial solution-treated MoNbTaW alloy is a homogeneous BCC solid solution with minimal pre-existing second phases.
The proposed intervention adds approximately 5 at.% Al to MoNbTaW.
The proposed intervention includes aging at 1000–1100 °C for several hours.
Adding Al and aging at 1000–1100 °C will produce fine, coherent L1₂ precipitates in the BCC matrix.
The L1₂ precipitates will be uniformly dispersed.
Al lowers the nucleation barrier for L1₂ phase formation during aging.
The L1₂ precipitates impede dislocation motion at high temperature through precipitation strengthening.
Precipitation strengthening will enhance creep resistance at 1100–1200 °C under sustained load.
The intervention will increase high-temperature creep resistance by approximately 20–30% relative to unmodified MoNbTaW.
The intervention will increase high-temperature yield strength by approximately 20–30% relative to unmodified MoNbTaW.
The modified alloy will maintain room-temperature tensile properties comparable to the baseline alloy.
The coherent and finely spaced precipitates will preserve room-temperature ductility.
The intervention will have only a minimal effect on overall density.
The coherent and finely spaced nature of the precipitates ensures that the density increase is negligible.
The baseline MoNbTaW alloy without Al and without controlled aging has lower high-temperature strength and creep resistance.
Extended high-temperature exposure or cyclic loading may cause behavior to deviate from the predicted improvement.
Competitive phase transformations may occur during prolonged high-temperature exposure and reduce strengthening effectiveness.

contradictions.description: The stated baseline is MoNbTaW without Al and without controlled aging, whereas the experimental control is described as Al-free but identically processed, implying that it receives the aging treatment. Thus, the experimental comparison does not exactly implement the declared baseline.
